title: Everyone Knows Something About Everything
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Meyer argues that one of the most important principles of teaching is that everyone knows something about everything, because all learning interacts with earlier knowledge. He contrasts the wish that students would simply absorb what a teacher says with the cognition that actually exists in classrooms. Early knowledge is both a responsibility, since students' experience is as essential as the teacher's, and a resource, as when a child describes a shape as bumpy and that idea can be developed into a rule. He criticizes most math curricula for opening units with formal adult definitions, using a textbook paragraph on circles as an example, and for having no room for early student thinking. Teachers who modify curricula are really creating room for that thinking, which he says makes teaching easier and learning more engaging.
points: All new learning interacts with prior knowledge, so a teacher is always building on something students already hold.
Student intuitions such as shapes being bumpy are a gift that can be steered toward mathematical ideas with simple questions.
Most textbooks open with polished adult definitions and so waste early student thinking.
Teacher curriculum modifications are better understood as creating room for early ideas than as making material more engaging, and curricula should not force that work onto teachers.
quotes: All learning interacts with earlier knowledge. So whatever you’re trying to teach an old kid right now is interacting with knowledge they developed as a young kid which is interacting with knowledge they developed as a very, very young kid and so on.

We might wish learning worked a different way, a way where I say stuff the way I understand it and then you immediately understand that stuff the same way I do no matter what you knew before I started saying stuff. But we go to the classroom with the principles of cognition we have not the principles of cognition we might want.

That early knowledge is a responsibility for teachers. We need to let students know that their knowledge and experience are as essential to their learning as their teacher’s knowledge and experience. But that early knowledge is a resource for teachers as well. It’s a gift. It makes teaching easier.
The failing of most math curricula is that they waste the gift of early student thinking.

The vast majority of math textbooks make no use of early student thinking. They make no room for it. Those textbooks share the formal, developed thinking of an adult and then ask students to develop their own ideas on those terms.

When teachers modify their curriculum, they’ll often describe their efforts to make it more “engaging.” But another name for what they’re doing is j”creating room,” creating room for early ideas from students and finding ways to treat those ideas like the resource, the gift, that they are. This makes teaching easier for the teacher. And, for the student, there are few experiences more engaging than experiencing some knowledgeable other person as deeply engaged in you.
